findings.evidence: Removing the financial penalty for late returns predictably increases both on-time return rates and overall program participation, which is the reason the pilot's return-rate and avoidance-survey results, taken together, support ending fines for the whole consortium rather than only the pilot branches. This relationship is documented in the Tri-County Library Data Cooperative's 2023 fines-elimination research brief, which reviewed return-rate data from fourteen library systems that eliminated fines between 2017 and 2022.
findings.fix: Either name a source that backs the participation half of the principle, or point directly to the pilot's own avoidance-survey finding as the backing for that half instead of folding it into a citation that, by its own description, covers return-rate data only.
findings.location: Why the Pilot Result Applies Systemwide section, first two paragraphs
findings.violation: The stated general principle has two parts, increased return rates and increased program participation, but the cited brief is described as reviewing only return-rate data. The participation half of the principle is left without a named study, standard, or precedent, so a reader who would not grant that half on sight has nothing to test it against, even though the return-rate half is backed.

findings.evidence: This recommendation applies to items returned within 60 days of their due date; items still unreturned past that window remain subject to the existing replacement-cost billing process, matching the return-rate pattern the pilot data actually established.
findings.fix: Either cite the specific pilot data point that establishes a 60-day return pattern, for example the share of eventual returns completed within 60 days, or drop the claim that the window matches the pilot's pattern and justify the cutoff on its own terms.
findings.location: Recommendation section, third paragraph (the 60-day carve-out sentence)
findings.violation: The sentence asserts that the 60-day window matches a pattern the pilot data established, but the pilot section (What the Pilot Showed) reports only an aggregate 16-month on-time-or-eventual return rate comparison, 94 percent versus 87 percent, and never reports any return-timing breakdown or a 60-day figure. A reader checking the cited grounds finds nothing that establishes this pattern, so the claim is an assertion rather than evidence a reader could check.

findings.evidence: A skeptic on the board points to overdue fines as a source of materials-replacement funding, and argues that eliminating them systemwide will leave a shortfall the consortium has not planned for. Consortium finance records show fine revenue covered under 2 percent of the annual materials budget over the last three fiscal years, and the four pilot branches absorbed the loss without a measurable change to their replacement-copy spending, so the shortfall the objection anticipates has not materialized where the policy has already been tried.
findings.fix: Add a paragraph addressing whether removing fines lengthens the time high-demand items are unavailable to other patrons, using data the pilot already collected such as hold-queue length or the gap between on-time and eventual returns, or explicitly acknowledge it as an open question the pilot did not measure.
findings.violation: The artifact raises and answers the revenue objection but never raises the availability objection its own grounds expose: the pilot's own on-time-or-eventual return rate metric concedes that some items are returned late rather than on time, which implies items may sit out of circulation longer once the fine deterrent is removed, a foreseeable access concern for other patrons. That second foreseeable challenge is never named or answered anywhere in the document.
